outcomes: The Cloud CLI works in a hosted agent session: the signed-in session wins over the workspace machine token, login hands its code to a host without a terminal, read commands build nothing, and a read-only cache credential stays quiet
nonGoals: Approving a device code on behalf of a person: the host hands the code to an approver
Changing what a machine token may read or write on the server
Choosing PUTNAMI_CLOUD_TOKEN over a usable signed-in session

text: When ~/.putnami/auth.json holds a usable session (a fresh access token, or a refresh token), every workspace command authenticates with it, even when PUTNAMI_CLOUD_TOKEN is set.
The workspace machine token is used only when no usable session is stored; no flag or variable chooses it over a usable session.
A run with no stored session behaves as before.
whoami and status name the credential the workspace commands use: the signed-in user, or PUTNAMI_CLOUD_TOKEN, and why.
--verbose prints one line naming the credential a workspace command used.
An authentication error of a workspace command names the credential that was refused, on a machine that holds both.

Under --output=jsonl, putnami cloud login writes one record with user_code, verification_uri, verification_uri_complete and expires_in before it waits for the approval, and the result record once the code is approved.
The record never carries the device code.
Under any structured output the human instructions are not written to stdout.
The cloud whoami, status, login and logout subcommands declare workspaceState none, so they answer without the workspace install and without restoring generated clients.

When core lists read-only at initialize, the cache provider echoes it for a session that cannot write: a workspace machine token, or the signed-in user's putnami cloud token --for cache recipe off a hosted run.
After the echo the provider prints no read-only line of its own, since core says it once.
A hosted run, a run credential, a metadata identity and every other token source are not declared read-only, and a refused write still closes the write path for the rest of the run.
